lead: The two readings meet at a table. Paul tells the Corinthians that the cup we bless and the bread we break are a sharing in the blood and body of Christ, and that because there is one bread, we who are many are one body. In John, Jesus takes five barley loaves, gives thanks, and feeds a great crowd, and nothing is lost. The bread that Christ gives makes the many one, and there is always enough.

set: Corinth was full of temples, and much of the meat sold in the market had first been offered to the gods. Feasts in temple dining halls were a normal part of social life. Some Corinthian Christians thought that, since idols are nothing, they could join in such meals without scruple (8:1–10). Paul has warned them with the example of Israel in the wilderness (10:1–13). Now he speaks of the Lord’s Supper: those who share in Christ’s table cannot also share in the table of idols.
str: vv. 14–15: flee idolatry; judge for yourselves.
vv. 16–17: the cup and the bread are a sharing in Christ’s blood and body; one bread, one body.
v. 18: Israel’s sacrifices make those who eat them partners in the altar.
vv. 19–21: the idol is nothing, but pagan sacrifice is partnership with demons: you cannot share both tables.
v. 22: do not provoke the Lord to jealousy.
kw: A Jewish name for the cup of wine over which the blessing was said at a festive meal. Jesus took such a cup at the Last Supper, and the Church blesses it still.
Paul draws a conclusion from the single loaf broken at the Supper: many share one bread, and so they become one body. The Eucharist does not only express the Church’s unity; it makes it.
An echo of the Song of Moses, where Israel “made me jealous with what is no god” (Deuteronomy 32:21). God’s jealousy is the love of a husband who will not share his bride with idols.
vv: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?
Paul does not argue for the Real Presence; he takes it for granted, and builds his warning on it. Because the bread is truly a sharing in Christ’s body, eating it binds us to him.
Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
Communion is never private. To receive Christ’s body is to be joined to all who receive it, the poor and the stranger included.
You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.
Faith asks for an undivided heart. Today the “other table” may be money, power or superstition, wherever we seek what only God can give.
ch: The Catechism quotes verses 16–17 to teach that the Eucharist makes the Church: those who receive it are united more closely to Christ, and Christ unites them to all the faithful in one body (CCC 1396). It also quotes St Augustine’s words to the newly baptized: if you are the body and members of Christ, it is your own mystery that is placed on the Lord’s table; be what you see, and receive what you are (in substance, Sermon 272; CCC 1396).

set: This is the only miracle of Jesus’ public ministry, apart from the Resurrection, that all four Gospels tell. John sets it near Passover (6:4), the feast of the Exodus and the manna, and on a mountain, as Moses received the Law on a mountain. The scene opens the whole chapter on the bread of life, and the crowd’s reaction, wanting to make him king, shows how easily a sign can be misunderstood.
str: vv. 1–4: setting: across the sea, a large crowd, the mountain, Passover near.
vv. 5–9: Jesus tests Philip; Andrew finds a boy with five barley loaves and two fish.
vv. 10–11: the people sit on the grass; Jesus gives thanks and distributes.
vv. 12–13: “Gather up the fragments”: twelve baskets left over.
vv. 14–15: “This is indeed the prophet”; they want to make him king; he withdraws alone.
kw: John calls Jesus’ miracles “signs”: works that point beyond themselves to who he is. The feeding is a sign of the bread of life that he will explain in the synagogue.

The pieces broken from the loaves. Very early Christian prayer used the same word for the broken Eucharistic bread (Didache 9). “So that nothing may be lost” recalls the Father’s will that none be lost (6:39).
The crowd recalls Moses’ promise that God would raise up a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15). Moses gave manna; here is one who gives bread in the wilderness.
vv: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are they among so many people?”

Barley bread was the food of the poor. Only John mentions the boy and the barley, which recalls Elisha feeding a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, with some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). Christ begins with the little that someone is willing to give.
Then Jesus took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated
Took, gave thanks, distributed: the words of every Eucharist. John’s first readers would hear in them the Lord’s Supper.
When they were satisfied, he told his disciples, “Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.”
God’s abundance is never wasteful. Twelve baskets, a number that recalls the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles: enough for the whole people of God.
When Jesus realized that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, he withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
They want a king who will fill their stomachs. Jesus is King, but not in that way; his throne will be the Cross (19:19).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the miracles of the multiplication of the loaves, when the Lord says the blessing, breaks and distributes the loaves through his disciples to feed the multitude, prefigure the superabundance of the unique bread of his Eucharist (CCC 1335). St Augustine remarks that God works greater wonders every day, when a few seeds multiply into whole harvests, but we no longer marvel at them; so in this miracle he did by his own hand what he does always in the fields, to awaken us to see him at work (in substance, Tractates on John 24).

qa: Why did Jesus withdraw when the crowd wanted to make him king?

He is King, but his kingdom is not of this world (18:36). The crowd wanted a ruler who would give bread and drive out the Romans. The Catechism notes that Jesus accepted the title of Messiah with reserve, because many of his contemporaries understood it in too human and political a sense (CCC 439). He would reveal his kingship on the Cross.
study: Paul says that because there is one bread, we who are many are one body. Whom do I find it hard to see as one body with me when we receive the Holy Qurbana together?
A boy gave five barley loaves, and Christ fed thousands. What small thing can I place in his hands today?
